utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'd ask the registry officer to notify Your Honours there are two matters I wish to raise before the witness resumes his evidence. The first is, I suppose, the two oral motions. The first is in relation to evidence the Defence counsel, Mr. Pisarevic, led yesterday from this witness. The second is in relation to an application I wish to make to cross-examine him as to an inconsistency. I'll come to the second one in a moment. The first one is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you slow down, Mr. Re, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise. I will slow down. The first one is in the Prosecution's submission a fairly serious matter relating to the date of the Crkvina massacre. Yesterday before the Trial Chamber, counsel for Mr. Zaric, Mr. Pisarevic, at page 17 of the LiveNote version led - when I said "led," I mean led in the most egregious fashion - from the witness the following evidence: Mr. Nikolic, now we shall move on to an event which happened in Crkvina on the 8th of May, 1992. The event in Crkvina is a crime which happened when 16 people were killed in a warehouse. How did you learn about this event? Over the page at page 18, I -- I didn't object at the time because it was too late. Mr. Pisarevic had already -- already deliberately raised the date of the 8th and had put it to the witness on the record about something happened -- happening on the 8th of May. At the following page I objected or sought clarification as to when Mr. Nikolic -- or Mr. Zaric informed Mr. Nikolic of the -- of the massacre. There was an exchange. At the bottom of page 18, Mr. Zaric -- I'm sorry, Mr. Pisarevic again said: Question: I told you we would be talking about the events of the 8th. Answer: On the 9th. Meaning Zaric told me on the 9th. Mr. Zaric then led -- sorry, Mr. Pisarevic then led again, put words in the witness's mouth. It was hopeless trying to object once the witness had already been told what the answer was supposed to be. Question: Yes. Tell us, when did Mr. Zaric inform you about the time and when did you talk with Djordjevic and Radovanovic and Todorovic? Answer: I think it was on the 9th, the 9th of May. Question: And it was early in the morning. That's Mr. Pisarevic putting words in the witness's mouth. No point in objecting because the evidence is already given by Mr. Pisarevic. Answer: He didn't get the answer he wanted. The answer was,"That was in the morning before noon." Now, the importance of this and what counsel did yesterday and in the Prosecution's submission can only be deliberate and in response to those two documents was to lead evidence which is contrary to the opening statement and Mr. Zaric's own records of interview with the Prosecutor. I take Your Honours to P140 -- 141 ter, at page 58 of the ter version. When the Prosecutor, Ms. Paterson, said to Mr. Zaric, "I'd like you to know --" she asked him, "I'd like to know what you know about the killing of the men in Crkvina on the 7th of May, 1992. Do you know, for example, why some of the men were being detained and transferred?" Mr. Zaric's answer was, "The case in Crkvina was one of the worst things that happened." And there's a fairly lengthy answer in which he does not challenge the date but it goes on further. At page 60, he describes, informing Mr. Nikolic, and he says, "Before 8.00 the next morning, that is, the 9th -- sorry, the 8th. I was there to speak to the security officer and Commander Nikolic." And goes on to say, describe how he informed Nikolic on the morning of the 8th about the Crkvina massacre. He then goes down the page to say, "I told you yesterday I spoke to --" sorry, he spoke to Nikolic. "I was given approval. I was told I could go the next day and speak to Colonel Maksimovic. He had been a high-ranking officer in the SSNO of Yugoslavia," et cetera. Down a bit further, "I told you yesterday I spoke to General Gligorovic and General Vasiljevic also attended the meeting. All this happened on the 9th of May." That's in Belgrade. And he refers back to the previous day, the previous statement of Mr. Zaric to the Prosecutor, at P140 ter, when at page 57, Mr. Zaric says, "In the beginning of May, it was the 9th of May, I was in Belgrade. I went to the SSNO, the security service of the SSNO," et cetera. "The reason I went there was because of the tragic incident that took place in Crkvina." Mr. Zaric's own case, his own statement was that the massacre took place on the 7th, he informed Mr. Nikolic on the morning of the 8th, and he went to -- Nikolic told him to go to Belgrade on the 9th of May. In Mr. Pisarevic's opening statement on the 24th of February, at transcript page 15.705, Mr. Zaric -- Mr. Pisarevic said of Mr. Zaric's records of interview or statements, "Upon his arrival, Zaric of his own free will decided to give to statement to the Prosecutor and spoke with the investigators on three occasions, not concealing anything and not avoiding any subject, no matter what it was. As always, Mr. Zaric was completely sincere, while providing the statements. These interviews have been tendered into evidence in this case. Many facts that were not known until then were in fact affirmed through the statement of Mr. Zaric, which speaks best about the approach of Mr. Zaric to these proceedings right from the very beginning. The aim of the Defence of Mr. Zaric is to bring up each one of these untrue claims by witnesses of the Prosecution - this is important - and to present evidence which would completely shed light on each such episode and confirm all that Mr. Zaric stated in his interview." And to confirm all that Mr. Zaric stated in his interview of course would be to not contest Mr. Zaric's own statement that the massacre occurred on the 7th. Now, in fact, of course it goes further because there was uncontested evidence given of the date of the massacre. It was in closed session. I refer Your Honours to the page number T11 -- it's transcript 11592 onwards. The cross-examination was in open session. That's by Mr. Pisarevic at transcript pages 11.625 to 11.636 on the 30th of July last year -- or sorry, the year before -- sorry, 2002. In that cross-examination, Mr. Pisarevic, counsel for Mr. Zaric, did not in any way challenge the date, the only date -- or the date which in the circumstances of that evidence was clearly reliable and uncontested evidence. There was no contest to the -- the date, no suggestion that the date was mistaken or it occurred on another day. It wasn't, in fact, until Mr. Nikolic or Mr. Zaric -- Mr. Pisarevic put words into Mr. Nikolic's mouth yesterday that there seemed to be any shift in the Defence case as to the date of the Crkvina massacre. The leading, and the Prosecution says it was outrageous leading in the circumstances by Mr. Pisarevic, had to have been intentional in the light of the two orders, P174 and P175 tendered into evidence yesterday, and the witness's evidence in relation to the dates and the subordination of those paramilitaries to him. And that's quite important, of course, to Mr. Nikolic because if those troops were subordinated to him on the 8th, as his evidence was, and in the morning, he would have been responsible for -- he would have been their superior officer in relation to any acts that they had committed. He would have been under a duty under Article 21 of the Yugoslav code to punish people under his command and under his effective control for acts that, according to Mr. Zaric's own statement in evidence, Mr. Nikolic must have already knew -- would have already known about. So my application in relation to that, having outlined the circumstances which led Mr. Pisarevic to put that evidence into the witness's mouth before the Trial Chamber, is that the Prosecution on an oral motion seeks -- requests the Trial Chamber to direct Defence counsel not to do that again, not to ask leading questions, especially in relation to changes in their case, in relation to things which were before or hitherto uncontested but contested in the most strange way possible by -- by a Defence counsel, lead counsel, suggesting another date to a witness in the context -- the context is something which is quite contested. That is my first application. The second one relates to the cross-examination of Mr. Nikolic himself and the evidence he has given. And it goes back to that same point. The Prosecution applied or made an application in relation to the evidence of, I think it was Mr. Omeranovic, to cross-examine the witness on the redacted portions of his 92 bis statement, only on the basis of prior inconsistent statement, not leading it as truth of the allegations contained therein but only as to inconsistencies and the witness's credit. Following Your Honours' oral ruling, the Prosecution filed a motion either for redetermination in the light of considered legal -- written legal arguments or requests for certification under Rule 73(B). That request was filed Friday week before last and is outstanding. Now, the issue -- obviously the reason why the Prosecution filed it was because we anticipated that the issue may reappear, and it has, before Your Honours have ruled on our request for redetermination. So I seek leave, Your Honours' leave, in the light of your previous ruling, to cross-examine Mr. Nikolic in relation to matters contained in paragraph -- in paragraph 42 -- or sorry, 44 of his redacted 92 bis statement, which was of course a statement which was a sworn statement, as to when Mr. Zaric told him about the Crkvina massacre. It contains an inconsistency between Mr. Zaric's record of interview and, of course, the evidence the witness gave yesterday, which of course brings me back to the whole point about Mr. Pisarevic suggesting not only a date but a time, early in the morning, which is inconsistent with the sworn statement of a witness whose statement he took and has actually brought to court. But it was redacted for the purposes of admission into evidence. These are very serious matters in my submission. So firstly, I seek the Trial Chamber's direction of -- to Defence counsel. And secondly, I seek leave to cross-examine as to the inconsistencies in paragraph 44 only as to the witness's credit and only on a prior inconsistent statement because he said -- because his evidence yesterday was different to matters which are contained in a statement which was sworn under 92 bis and has a declaration under 92 bis (B) appended to it. Those are my two applications, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I address the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, and thank you. To begin with, I'd like to say that all this that my learned friend spoke about could appear as the OTP sees it, but it is absolutely not true. The witness's statement, which was certified as far back as February and was already as far back as December 2002, in the part which was stricken out, that is, paragraph 44, the witness testifies about this date which he's aware. The existence of an order that the Prosecutor refers to was disclosed to the Defence a day before the witness came to testify. The Prosecution never disclosed this order to Mr. Zaric's Defence. We simply did not know that the Prosecution had those orders in their possession. And since I did not know that, I could not start construing something in August, October, or a few months earlier. So my question was asked because the witness said in his testimony that it had happened on the 8th of May. True, Mr. Zaric said that it was on the 7th at the time of his interview, but the Chamber should then establish which date is correct. We also have testimonies of other witnesses who said that it was on the 8th of May. I never had any intention or any need at all to try to hint anything to the witness, to lead him, to try to make him provide a specific answer. There is no foundation to this Prosecution's claim. Above all, because the Prosecutor is aware that this order was disclosed to the Defence a day before only, and that was the first time that we ever saw it. And I think that as regards to the witness, my learned friend can examine him about all the facts. The witness has made a solemn declaration and he should answer the questions. However, I believe the Prosecutor is using too many words to explain something, and very often what he explains here or trying to construe here looks more like a closing argument than anything else. But there will be other time to go into what is true and what is not true, what has been proven and what hasn't. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may. Just two words. Just two words, please. I'd like to suggest to the Chamber with regard to this date of the massacre in Crkvina, of course the Trial Chamber will establish facts. But this same OTP, which claims that it happened on the 7th of May, has indicted Mr. Seselj and in his indictment - and he's also charged with the massacre in Crkvina - it says the 8th of May, so that I merely wish to draw attention to that fact that that is one of the claims of the Prosecution. I merely wish to draw attention to that particular fact. And as for the cross-examination which has to do with the drafted statement made under 92 bis and the Trial Chamber at the time when I examined Djordje Tubakovic and the Prosecution in relation to this said in brief we never pronounced ourselves on that. But I will just mention with reference to an earlier decision of the Trial Chamber that one cannot measure the consistency against something that does not exist. It is simply not possible, and I believe that the Trial Chamber should abide by its earlier decision that something like that cannot be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I briefly respond to just two matters Mr. Pisarevic raised. The first one is he said just then the witness referred to the date in paragraph 44. Yes, he did. But he said, "I remember that on the night of 8th/9th May, 1992. Simo Zaric informed me that a horrific crime had occurred." My point was that Mr. Pisarevic yesterday tried to put words in his mouth that it occurred the next morning. The second point is in relation to disclosure of those two orders. It wasn't the day before. It came about as a result of the Prosecution doing its search in relation to Colonel Nikolic and the two documents coming up there. We disclosed them on Thursday, the 9th of August -- sorry, the 9th of April, which was the first opportunity we had to disclose them to the Defence, having only found them on Wednesday. And in any event, the witness testified yesterday that he knew these documents, I think the words he used were off by heart. There's no mention of those orders in his 92 bis statement anywhere. He says they weren't subordinated to him. There's no mention of the fact that he used these paramilitaries or -- sorry, or police, as he calls them, in any actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will rise for 15 minutes to deal with the oral motions. --- Break taken at 9.23 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: On the oral motions raised by the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber has observed that the first point on different dates given at different stages of the proceedings, that on different dates of any event that are given by the witnesses is normally a common feature in criminal trials. It is a matter for evaluation of the evidence at the end of the trial in order to determine the date, if it is material. If a witness is misled or is led by counsel who puts a leading question to the witness, that again raises the question of how much weight should be attached to the evidence of the witness, who almost in all cases has actually made a solemn declaration to tell the truth. In this case, the Prosecution can still cross-examine the witness on the date if it is material to them. On the orders which are now exhibits P174 and P175, disclosed to the Defence before the witness started to give evidence, if it was material to the Defence, as they claim, that these orders -- these exhibits were disclosed to them late, they should have raised an objection. And depending on the factors, the Trial Chamber would have been able to rule whether or not those exhibits could be put to the witness. Of course, counsel at all times when examining a witness in chief should avoid leading questions. On the second oral motion, to use matters in paragraphs that are struck out, even for credibility purposes, the Trial Chamber's stance remains the same, that no such matters can be resurrected at any stage for any purposes. On the written motion on a similar matter raised by the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber will give its ruling in due course. So the proceedings will continue. The cross-examination can continue. And the witness should be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. You are cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Re: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikolic. I will continue from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 17th of April, 1992, you issued orders for weapons to be collected, and you gave evidence yesterday, in Bosanski Samac, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, to a part of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You issued the orders to Mr. Antic and Mr. Savic, that's Jovo Savic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I issued the order to Mr. Radovan Antic, and he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Antic delegated the supervision of the weapons collection to Mr. Zaric and Mr. Tadic, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And it goes by itself. To the security office, that is, those whose -- who have it as part of their job description.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Antic issued those orders -- or sorry, delegated the supervision to Mr. Zaric and Mr. Tadic on the 17th of April, 1992, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 17th of April, after I tasked him with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 17th of April, 1992, Mr. Tadic and Mr. Zaric were both involved in the supervision of the weapons collection, based upon your order, in Bosanski Samac, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave evidence yesterday of the intelligence which you were provided about the illegal arming which was occurring prior to the takeover on the 17th of April. I'm just saying that to lead you back. You remember that evidence, don't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, of course -- and your evidence was yesterday that you tasked or delegated him with intelligence gathering or collection in the region. Mr. Zaric was a trusted and reliable source of information to you, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was his job because of the place that he had in the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some people do their jobs badly. What I'm suggesting to you is that Mr. Zaric was a trusted and reliable gatherer or source of information to you and others in the command who needed it, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information provided by Mr. Zaric we forwarded to the command of the 17th Corps, and there were people who were competent to establish whether this information was accurate or not, half true or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about your assessment of the quality of the information that Mr. Zaric provided. As far as you're concerned, was his information accurate, reliable, and trustworthy?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my mind, yes, he was a trustworthy person. One could rely on the information he provided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He had excellent contacts in the Samac municipality, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a man of prestige. He knew the job from before and he had good contacts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These contacts spread way beyond Samac, didn't they? They spread even to Belgrade, where he had excellent contacts there as well.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is, of course, one of the reasons why you sent him, as opposed to anyone else, to Belgrade in relation to the Crkvina massacre, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric had provided reliable and accurate information to you prior to the takeover in relation to the illegal arming of all of the nationalist or national parties, hadn't he? SDS, HDZ, and SDA.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of the moment when the 4th Detachment started to operate, he supplied this information to my security assistant, Mr. Makso Simeunovic regularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the information you had, all three parties were equally guilty of illegally arming themselves before the takeover, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the overview which we saw here yesterday, in the territory of Bosanski Samac we didn't have any information that the SDS was also procuring weapons. But I think that yes, there was information that all the three parties were illegally arming themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. The witness's answer has not been separated from the question. The witness's answer begins on page 14, line 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think that should be corrected, to show that the witness had answered the question, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say there was information -- or sorry, I'll put that in quotes. When you say there was "information that all the three parties were arming themselves," you of course mean the HDZ, the SDA, and SDS, don't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, the takeover was led or the takeover, according to your evidence, was led by the Crisis Staff, which was led by the SDS, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff, yes, led the takeover of power. Now, whether the SDS ran the Crisis Staff, I cannot give you a reliable answer because basically I wasn't interested in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew that Dr. Simic was on -- was the president of the Crisis Staff and a very prominent SDS member. You knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew that Mr. Todorovic, the chief of police, was also on the Crisis Staff and an SDS member, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Ninkovic, Bozo Ninkovic, likewise on the Crisis Staff and an SDS member?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bozo Ninkovic -- no, I mean, I cannot remember who that man is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Mirko Jovanovic? You knew that he was an SDS member and on the Crisis Staff, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course Dr. Simic -- your evidence was that Dr. Simic, Mr. Jovanovic, and Mr. Todorovic, all three SDS members, came to the meeting in relation to the arrival of the police, volunteers, paramilitaries, call them what you will, from Serbia just after their arrival.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course they were the people who told you that the paramilitaries were -- or these police, as you've described them, were under their control, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what Mr. Todorovic said primarily. And the rest didn't deny it during the course of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, police from the Serbian Republic of Krajina had no business being in the municipality of Bosanski Samac in April 1992, did they, sir? Especially not armed and in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered yesterday that the explanation of my corps commander was, after I had submitted my report, that there is a certain agreement. I hadn't seen that agreement between Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina on mutual assistance. And that it is on that basis that this group was sent to Bosanski Samac and at the request of Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the things that you, as the local JNA tactical -- 17th Tactical Group commander was very concerned about was the illegal arming and the potential for ethnic unrest or clashes in the period leading up to the takeover; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took all measures to stop illegal arming. I worked within the scope of my own possibilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you met Dr. Simic, Mr. Jovanovic, and Mr. Todorovic shortly after the arrival of these police, as you call them, from the Republika Srpska Krajina, neither -- they didn't hold an official position connected to the policing of the democratically elected Municipality of Bosanski Samac, did they?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had police IDs. And now, whether they had any powers, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the police or paramilitaries who came. I'm talking about Simic, Jovanovic, and Todorovic. Neither of those three had any official capacity in relation to policing in the democratically elected Municipality of Bosanski Samac, did they? That's as of about April the 10th, 11th, 12th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you've already agreed they were all SDS members, and you were concerned about illegal arming of the parties, and they were -- they said that they had put these people under their command. A week later there was a takeover, and you say by the police, as you call them, and the Crisis Staff. My question is: You sent Mr. Zaric into the SUP after you spoke to Mr. Todorovic to allow him to interrogate people in relation to the illegal arming. That was your evidence yesterday. Now, the only people held in that police station were Muslims and Croats, weren't they, at that stage?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you say "for the most part," how many Serbs were there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was a Serb or two there. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Your orders were to Zaric to go and interrogate, that is, to interrogate the Muslims and Croats, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order was not to interrogate the Muslims and Croats. The order was to use his best judgement to see who would the best people be to have information about illegal arming, and then he should talk to these people and inform the command of the 17th Tactical Group about that. So not at a single moment did I distinguish between people on ethnic, religious, or racial grounds. This is shown by my own security detail. One was a Serb, one was a Croat, and one was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. But you've already agreed that only Muslims and Croats, bar possibly one or two Serbs, were actually held in the police station, and the police station was the place where you told Mr. Zaric by -- Mr. Todorovic to go and seek information, that is, interview or interrogate people. Clearly he wasn't going to be interviewing any Serbs in that police station, was he, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there weren't any there, there was no reason for him to talk to them. However, if there was a Serb, I mean, he would have had to talk to everyone who could have possibly been involved in the illicit arming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's exceedingly hypothetical in relation to the possibility of a Serb being there and him speaking to that person. You, of course, didn't issue him with any orders to interview Serbs in Bosanski Samac who had been involved with illegal arming, did you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I issued him an order to talk to everyone who he suspects of having been involved in illegal arming. I did not distinguish on ethnic grounds at all. And I explained yesterday. The reason for this was that in the -- among the officers of the 17th Tactical Group, we realised that there were people who were involved in illegal arming and that was a tactic. We wanted to find out who was behind this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me just take you back to the question I was asking you. You've already agreed that Jovanovic, Simic, and Todorovic were SDS members and that there was information that the SDS had been involved in illegally arming. What specific orders did you issue to Mr. Zaric to interview SDS people in relation to illegal arming? And if you issued the orders, where can we find a copy of these orders?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me start my answer from the end. Everything that was commanded in Tactical Group 17 are official documents, and it stayed behind at Tactical Group 17. All the documents can be found there, I assume. There is no reason for them to be anywhere else. As for this, I repeat once again, I did not tell Mr. Zaric to talk to Muslims or to Serbs or to Croats. I told him to speak to persons who he suspects of possibly having participated in the illegal arming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you're aware, Mr. Zaric only interviewed or interrogated people held prisoner in the SUP.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were only Muslims and Croats; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I did not go into the SUP. And I am not in a position to establish who all the people detained were there. I just know that later when we took over a number of prisoners and we transferred them outside our area of responsibility, that they were Muslims and Croats for the most part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's a fair conclusion to draw that the people you took from there on the 26th of April just all happened to be Muslims and Croats, that it was only Muslims and Croats being held there, isn't it, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first conclusion is quite correct. The people we transferred were Muslims and Croats. And now, whether anybody stayed behind, that is something I don't know. For example, Izet Izetbegovic stayed behind. He was a Muslim. We did not succeed in transferring him to the other side in that group. I assume that some other prisoners were left behind as well, but I cannot corroborate that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, of course, provided you in the command with reports of his interrogations or interviews, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He submitted this report to the Chief of Security, and then we together analysed this at the level of the staff, or rather, the command of the tactical group. And then we sent this analysis to our superior command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He sent them through Maksimovic, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he handed it over to Maksimovic. Yes. Yes. To Makso Simeunovic, because he was Chief of Security. So this is the top leadership of the command, and then we discussed it there, and then we sent it on to our superior command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you discussed it, you were aware of the contents of all the reports that Mr. Zaric submitted, and you were also interested in who these people were who had been illegally arming, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was mostly aware of the reports. Although, according to our rules, the security organ does have the right to use certain information at his own discretion. So there's always the possibility that according to one's official capacity or, rather, one's specific job, that information can be provided along those lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: None of the reports that Mr. Zaric provided to you through Mr. Maksimovic were in relation to Serbs, that is, the interview or interrogation of Serbs in the police station or anywhere else, were they?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, interviews could not be conducted in that way with people who were in positions of authority. Whereas, it was possible to interview persons who were detained in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is your answer that Mr. Zaric did not provide any reports of interviews with any SDS or Serbs in relation to the illegal arming?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no, if this does not mean that perhaps those who had taken over power and authority had not been illegally armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said Mr. Zaric was supposed to, as far as you were concerned, conduct his investigations without any ethnic prejudice or any ethnic bias, interview all parties concerned who may have been illegally arming themselves. What I suggest to you: That if Mr. Zaric only provided you with reports on the interrogations or interviews of Muslims and Croats, he couldn't have been doing his job according to your orders, could he, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, yes. Although, I would not dare claim that in these particular pieces of information that were sent, a Serb or two were not mentioned. After all, one of the smugglers who was later sentenced was a Serb who was a member of the JNA, and he did take part in this smuggling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your experience -- I withdraw that. The police and the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992, the first half of 1992, before the takeover, were separate entities, weren't they? The police had civilian duties; the military had military duties.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. However, the police, objectively speaking, in every conceivable way, specifically in Bosanski Samac, cooperated with groups that were arming themselves, notably the HDZ and the SDA. Probably with the others too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I wasn't asking you that, so please don't throw those three things in. I'm talking about jurisdictional matters. The police had quite separate legal jurisdictional duties to the military before the takeover in Bosnia -- sorry, in Bosanski Samac in 1992, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The police, of course, were concerned with -- sorry, I withdraw that. The role of the police, as in any normal society, was of civilian law and order enforcement and protection, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The police in Bosanski Samac didn't wear camouflage uniforms in the course of their normal duties, did they, sir, as the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not wear camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nor, of course, did they paint their faces black; did they, sir, in the normal course of their civilian police duties?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course they didn't wear patches or labels, such as white eagles, did they, in the normal course of their civilian policing duties?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or patches of wolves or tigers. Police didn't wear those in the course of their normal civilian policing duty, did they, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Police, of course, normal civilian police in Bosanski Samac in -- up till April 1992 didn't go on training missions with JNA or paramilitaries subordinated to the JNA, did they, sir? It would have been completely outside the normal policing duties, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police did not train with the JNA. The JNA trained on its own, and the police --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just repeat the last part of your sentence. You said the JNA trained on its own and the police -- we just missed the last part. Just please repeat the last part, from "and the police."

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the police carried out its own duties and its training according to its own plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The civilian police didn't have access to military helicopters either, did they, sir? This is in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And an 82-millimetre platoon or mortar platoon comprises about -- normally between four and six weapons and 15 to 20 men, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 128-mortar battery is normally between four and six men with four to six or eight weapons, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had four to six weapons, according to the establishment. Most often four. And the battery was supposed to have, say, about 40 men, tentatively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a 128-millimetre rocket launcher battery comprised about four weapons and 20 to 25 men, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a mortar battery does not exist in the JNA. If you're talking about 128-millimetre calibres, that refers to multiple rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I'm referring to, the multiple rocket launchers. And I'm suggesting that that is normally about four weapons and 20 to 25 men in the battery. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The platoon -- the things I've just referred to, the 82-millimetre platoon, 128-millimetre mortar battery, and the rocket launcher battery, are all, of course, artillery accompaniments to troops in battle, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are combat units. Artillery units have multiple rocket launchers, and infantry units have mortars of 60 and 82 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in an attack in which you divide the attacker -- the attacking troops into columns, the mortar batteries and platoons support each of the attacking columns, don't they, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Invariably in attack and in defence artillery support is organised among other forms of support. It is engaged or not engaged, depending on the actual situation involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the column commander, if there are columns in an attack, directs the mortar batteries and the mortar -- and the platoons where to fire; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. Artillery support is commanded by the person who is commanding the operation, or rather, these combat operations. Commanders of columns or echelons can request fire against certain targets, but they need not receive this kind of fire support.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If battle plans -- if you draw up battle plans and they show that the column is being supported by an 82-millimetre platoon or 128-millimetre mortar battery or 128-millimetre multiple round rocket launcher battery, those are going into battle supporting the attacking columns, aren't they, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But their fire is organised on the basis of the approval issued by the person who is commanding the combat operation. Not just anybody can use this for engaging targets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The column commander, if these units are -- if these platoons or batteries are supporting the column, can direct or does direct -- give directions as to where the platoon or battery should direct their fire; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of an echelon or column can engage independently, that is to say, on the basis of his own decision, only that which is under his direct command. If mortars of 60 millimetres or 82 millimetres are under his direct command, then he can request fire from these particular weapons and decide on that. As for bigger calibres, multiple rocket launchers, they are never under the command of an echelon or column; they are always under the command of the person who is in charge of the combat operation, who commands it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The column commander can direct where they fire. The column commander has to be experienced in warfare because of the consequences of directing fire in the wrong direction. You'd agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would rephrase that a bit. The column commander can point out the target and ask for that target to be engaged if fire had come from that target, and the commander of the mortar unit or of the artillery unit is professionally trained to target that particular objective and also to destroy it if necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you wouldn't place police officers, that is, police officers who deal with civilian structure of society in charge of columns which have supporting platoons and mortar batteries in a battle, would you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is why I did not put them in charge of that. I explained yesterday that a request for engaging police went through the organs of the corps command to the civilian authorities. As for the engagement of these people, commanders were those with certain experience. However, artillery fire is not something that they are involved in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Crni and Lugar, according to your descriptions yesterday of the people who arrived in Batkusa were - this is at page 8 of the transcript yesterday - police officers who deal with civilian structure of society. That's how you described Crni and Lugar and their colleagues yesterday. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I described them as members of the police, partly members of the Serb police, partly members of the police of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, who were trained in the area around Ilok.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the orders we -- I showed you yesterday and we put into -- to evidence, dated the 7th of May, 1992, clearly put Crni as the commander -- sorry, Lugar as the commander of a column called Crni which had an 82-millimetre platoon and multiple rocket launcher battery supporting him. That doesn't make sense in terms of your evidence that these people were police officers. You wouldn't put a police officer in charge of a column accompanied by an 82-millimetre platoon and multiple rocket launcher, would you, sir, and send them into battle? It would be the grossest dereliction of your command, wouldn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to clarify things. These people, Lugar and Crni, they were in charge of ordering units -- commanding units such as platoons or companies, and they were not able to command other units because that was in the hands of the other people who were commanding those operations. With regards to requests to engage members of the police and during the conversation I had with Mr. Todorovic, he insisted that if he gives me members of the police, he wanted that his own men command those members of the police, meaning the men who are commanders anyways. I had nothing against it because those tasks they were doing were objectively, if you will, infantry -- of infantry nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll take our break and continue at 11.00 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, I would just like to inform the Trial Chamber about some information. Mr. Simo Zaric has to leave tomorrow and he has to go to a hospital, and he is not going to be able to attend the proceedings. Since the Defence of Mr. Zaric has also in store another witness who's been waiting for his turn for nine days and it is Mr. Vaso Antic, and since Mr. Zaric is not ready to waive his right to be present during his defence, I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to see if it is possible to finish with the witness Mr. Antic today, bearing in mind the fact that the Trial Chamber has given a decision that Mr. Antic will be examined for an hour during the chief examination and an hour for his cross-examination, meaning two hours in whole. I would like to request and ask the Trial Chamber to take the necessary measures that the members of the OTP, bear in mind that you have given them a certain delay or a certain time, and if that would be the case, we would be able to finish today. If not, we would face the following situation, that Mr. Antic will have to come back to The Hague. This is all I wanted to inform the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber has actually been considering the time that was allotted for cross-examination and has allowed the Prosecution to go over that by half an hour. And in view of the importance of this witness, the Trial Chamber will allow the Prosecution another half hour to wind up their cross-examination. As to whether or not that will allow us to complete the other witness, that will remain to be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard that, Mr. Nikolic. I want you to give the shortest possible answers to my questions which I will try to make as precise as possible. Yesterday -- I withdraw that. The action in relation to the clearing of the corridor to Brcko, that occurred on the 10th of May, didn't it? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took place on the 8th of May, and on the 10th of May we deblocked the road towards Modrica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's in the area of -- was that in the area of Milosevac?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we speak to the road going towards Brcko, we are talking about the direction of Gorica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vidovica, no?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not Vidovica. It's the direction that you take from Loncari going to going towards Gorica going in the direction of Brcko. That's the order -- there is a mistake in that order, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, a moment ago, yes or no questions, please. Now, what I'm just asking you: The fighting in the direction of Modrica, was that in the area of Kladari?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is approximately that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Garovac?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Garovac, yes, well, I cannot really tell you exactly which villages were around there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Modrica?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you the whole direction, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's around Modrica. The fighting there occurred on the 10th, is that right, the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. On the 10th of May, in the morning we started the attack and the attack was over at about 10.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, were there any other attacks before you left Bosnia in that particular area, the area referred to in that order which you looked at yesterday?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other very serious combat operations around, Vidovica, Kopanica, there were also other serious combats around the area of village of Grebnice and also around the village of -- around, actually, Bosanski Samac from the direction of the River Sava and Prud.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The police that you used in the various actions were known as members of a special battalion, weren't they? When you used them in battle, they were called a special battalion; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were divided into groups, and you will see in the order that you can see such-and-such a group with members of the special battalion or special company, if you will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric informed you of the Crkvina massacre and he went to Belgrade the day after he informed you of that, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you gave evidence that Mr. Todorovic and you had both received orders - I'm quoting from the transcript at page 36 - "that I could place at my disposal the forces that I needed." I want to ask you: Who gave you these orders? I want you to answer it as precisely as possible. Who gave you those orders? Firstly who. Then I'll come to what the orders were. All right? In that order.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my command, the command of the 17th Corps. And for Mr. Todorovic, he was supposed to get this message from the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next question: When did you receive those orders that you could place at the disposal any forces you needed? Just the date, please, as best as you can do.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately around the 5th or the 6th of May. Then on the 7th of May, the planification began and also the preparing of documents began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive orders in writing; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part of the orders, they arrived through the fax, and it was a coded -- coded orders. Those were coded orders. Whereas, the other ones arrived by way of --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was a way of yes or no --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oral orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. That was a yes or no answer. Was it in writing? Answer: Yes. What did the orders say?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the orders we could read the following approximately, that there was an agreement -- an agreement was reached, and that it was possible to place all the necessary means in order to carry out the task for the following reason: That the JNA didn't exist any more and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was formed and there was the army of the federal -- the federal army existed, and we were orphans, if you will, with regards to the army. So we had the Territorial Defence of the Republika Srpska and the police of the Republika Srpska. And if you look at the orders, you will see that I have gathered all the information that I was able to gather in order to carry out this mission. And not -- it's not a mission of clearing, but it was a task --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stop. My question was: What did the order say? It said there was an agreement. Who -- I just want a simple answer. Who signed the orders you received on the 5th or 6th of May, or the 7th? Who signed them? That's all I want to know.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The orders that I received were signed by the commander of the 17th Army Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that at the time it was Commander General Nedeljkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said an agreement was reached, the order referred to an agreement being reached. What did the order say about who the agreement was between, the parties, please, the parties to the agreement referred to in the order?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood your question. I will not try to go in depth. There was an agreement reached between the members of the JNA on the one hand -- sorry, the VRS and the authorities of Republika Srpska, and through that order it was agreed upon what I just told you of earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your evidence yesterday was of soldiers assisting people to leave -- sorry, moving prisoners from the Bosanski Samac TO to Brcko. That was about the last few days of April 1992. And your evidence was that Mr. Zaric told you of terrible things that had been happening to those prisoners in the police station. Do you remember that evidence, don't you? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric had told you who the people -- I withdraw that. Mr. Zaric had told you that it was the police, as you called them, from Serbia who were committing these atrocities against the prisoners with Mr. Todorovic's active encouragement, hadn't he? That's what Mr. Zaric told you.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to clarify. He told me that the police, with the encouragement of Todorovic is mistreating the people and there were already -- that there was even one man who was killed. But if you're talking about the 24th of April, it happened on the 26th of April. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm interested in the information. Zaric told you that the police, that is, the people from Serbia - that's what I'm calling the police, because you're calling the police - were the ones that had been mistreating the prisoner, didn't he? Before the 26th of April, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me that those were men from Serbia. He told me the police, as far as I remember. I cannot quote literally what was told to me, but it was the police, and they belonged to those forces, and those were probably the ones who participated in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "belonged to those forces," you mean the ones who came in the helicopters from Krajina. They're the ones Mr. Zaric was talking about, wasn't it -- weren't they?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those men were part of the Serb police of the Municipality of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo, and those were those men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Despite Mr. Zaric informing you of the murder and the mistreatment and your own role in moving prisoners away from these men, you used these very same men in combat on the 8th of May, didn't you, Mr. Antic -- I'm sorry, Mr. Nikolic? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it is very simple to explain the reasons for this. Those men who were there, some of them had ranks, very important ranks, and they participated in combat activities. And even that meant that they had had experience, and up until that time there was no crime committed, so I didn't have any reason to believe that one of them was a criminal, and this is the reason why I put them in command. With regards to the tactical group, we were looking for somebody to command it. We didn't know who because the whole system was in a very shabby state, and so we chose people with experience. Each of these men were followed by the work of the command of the tactical group. So nobody could commit any kind of activity without us controlling them. And during those combat activities, I can confirm to you that no crime was committed and nothing that was in violation of humanitarian rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the question --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Human rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just spoke over the interpreter. The question I was asking you was: Zaric had told you and you knew yourself that these men from Serbia had committed very, very serious crimes in the TO and the police station, yet you still used these same men, that is, collectively, in your battle. It's a simple yes or no. You used those men, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of these men, yes, I used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you make a report when Mr. Zaric informed you about the Crkvina massacre; yes or no? That's all I want to know. Did you make a report?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A written report; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A written report, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you referred to that report in preparing yourself to give evidence here?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that report with me. I don't even have one single document with me. When I changed function, I also gave all the documents. The only documents that I saw were the documents that you showed me here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, again that was a no answer. The question was: Have you referred to it? The answer is no. You see?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all right. That's all right. When was the first time that you had to recall the date of the 8th of May in relation to these proceedings? When was the first time in relation to following when it happened, did you -- following the 8th of May, 1992 that you actually had to recall it for these proceedings? Was it recently?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that date because it's a specific date. I remember that date. I remember the 26th. It was also an important date, and also other dates which meant something to me. But I must say that there are a lot of dates that I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric in his statements to the Prosecutor, there were three records of interview or statements to the -- interviews with the Prosecutor in evidence -- agreed that the massacre took place on the 7th, that he informed you on the morning of the 8th, and he went to Belgrade on the 9th of May, 1992. That's what Mr. Zaric has said to the Prosecutor, and it's in evidence. That's different to what you say, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I was informed on the 8th in the afternoon -- or rather, the 9th in the morning, and this is why I sent Mr. Zaric to Belgrade that very day. It was on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've given several different versions now. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber again when Mr. Zaric informed you. Yesterday you said it was before midday on the 9th. Earlier today you said that Mr. Zaric went to Belgrade the next day. Now you've said, "I was informed on the 8th in the afternoon -- or rather, the 9th in the morning, and this is why I sent Mr. Zaric to Belgrade the same day. It was on the 9th of May." Which is the correct version of when you were informed and when you sent Mr. Zaric to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I got the information in the night between the 8th and the 9th and that Zaric went to Belgrade on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's version number three, sir. The 9th -- the night of the 8th or 9th --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly right now. Let's say maybe in the morning on the 9th, and that's why Zaric went to Belgrade right after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Mr. Pisarevic suggested to you yesterday it was early in the morning, you said no, it was before midday. You didn't say to him at the time, I'm not sure about the time, Mr. Pisarevic, I just think it was the morning. You didn't say that yesterday, did you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still don't know the right time. I'm just giving you an approximation. I cannot really tell you that I got the information at 6.00 a.m. or at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've got no reason to disbelieve what Mr. Zaric said in his statements -- two statements to the Prosecution about the -- about when he informed you and when he went to Belgrade, do you, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That event, I recall it as I explained it to you. I don't know what Mr. Zaric stated precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could help by telling the Trial Chamber where you were when Mr. Zaric informed you.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that I was at my command post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you supposed, is it that you've got no memory of it and you just think that's where you must have been?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part of my time, I was at the command post, and all the informations would get to the command post in Pelagicevo. So this is why I can say that it was probably in Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling the Trial Chamber you have no independent memory now, 11 years later, of him actually telling you but you're just assuming that because you were in command and a terrible thing happened and it was Zaric who told you, it must have been at that command post but you can't quite remember when it was? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say that it is almost impossible that he may have told me this just like that, orally. So an official place for all official conversations took place at the command post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm just asking you is: Is it true that -- is it the case that you now have no independent memory and you're just assuming it must have been at the command post? That's all I'm asking you. Your memory is gone. You just remember Zaric told you, and you assume it must have been at the command post because that's where you -- where you thought you would have been?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am almost sure that I was there, but it is quite possible that after 11 or 12 years I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you can't remember whether it was night or day either, can you, when Mr. Zaric told you this?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that at that time I didn't get much sleep, so that I can't really say whether it was night or day, and I think it is well nigh impossible to give a precise answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which of course leads you to the date. If you can't say where you were or whether it was night or day, you've got the same difficulties in remembering the precise date that he told you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I mean, this date stuck in my memory. I mean, one remembers something and one forgets other things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric wrote a book about his war experiences. Have you read his book?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was given the book as a present. I've read it. Mr. Zaric wrote this book expounding his point of view. That is how he saw things, I guess. There are many things in it that I do not recall, and there are also quite possibly many things that I might add to what he said in this book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He refers to you in the book, and he -- he wrote about the transfer of prisoners from [as said] Brcko in that book, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, so he did. Although, I told you yesterday that when the prisoners were transferred from my area of responsibility to Brcko, they simply ceased to be my concern because another unit and a different command took over the care for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Mr. Re, but in your question it reads "from." It should be "to."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, I correct that. I meant to Brcko. That is, from the TO to Brcko. That's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in his book -- it's page 176 of the English, 175/176 and I'm paraphrasing. He said it was for humanitarian reasons and in addition it was to -- a further interrogation of the people -- or some of the people who were suspects, and that was the removal of them from civilian to military custody to enable further interrogation of them. And that's -- that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My chief objective was to take them over and take them out of Bosanski Samac to prevent any terrorising of those people. Who later on investigated those people, who accommodated them, and how, that is something that I do not really know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, the time is up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that wasn't quite half an hour, Your Honour. We started at nine minutes past. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. The time is up. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour. I just wish to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you just ask your last question, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. The area I wish to ask him about is the command of the paramilitaries. In matters in Mr. -- I could do that in what I thought was the time remaining. This is the reason I'd done it this way. In relation to Mr. Zaric's record of interview and P127 as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please wind up, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to ask you about control of the paramilitaries. Mr. Zaric, in his record of -- or his statements to the Prosecutor - and I'm referring to P140 ter at page 54 and page 55 - says that you, Commander Nikolic -- he asked you, I'm sorry, what should be done about the paramilitary groups, that's those police. And after a couple of days you said that you were putting them under your command. That's in April, a few days after they arrived. And he said, "I would like to tell you, Prosecutor, the way I saw Mr. Nikolic until that very moment, I always saw him as a great Yugoslav." Mr. Zaric in his record of interview with the Prosecutor said that you said that you had put the paramilitaries under your command. Is that true or untrue?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said anything like that. In my statement, I said who received this group of paramilitaries, who fed them. Doesn't it look unnatural to you? Somebody receives them, he gives them to drink and to eat, and then I'm responsible for it? I mean, it makes no sense. I never put that group under my command. And I engaged them on such occasions when I was authorised to do so by my command, because the competencies of the 17th Tactical Group did not include that. I had no right to do that, as there was no state of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 73 of P140 ter - that's his interview with the Prosecutor on the 1st of April, 1998 - he said, in relation to Crni, who was very close to Stevan Todorovic and the police, "At some point, he was also made commander of the battalion and at some point his superior was Nikolic - that's you - for a very short time before he left for Yugoslavia." That's what Mr. Zaric said. He said that the -- Crni was under your command for some point before you left Yugoslavia. Is that true or untrue?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. Crni was never under my command, and I was never under his command. So that when I left, Crni organised a military coup, removed the commander who had taken the duty over from me, and assumed the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's as far as I can go in that time. Although, I'd just like to say for the record there were issues with the takeover and the arrest which the Prosecution wished to explore but understands the time limits and couldn't -- and also in relation to several miscellaneous issues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re, the time was given to the Prosecution to deal with the matters they thought were important. And inserting the time, the Trial Chamber did look at the issues which this witness covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. There's just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We even extended the time because of the importance of this witness, so there should be no more argument about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Your Honours please, I'm not arguing. I just wish to place on the record I also wished to ask him about Exhibit P164, a comment in his video, and those were the matters which I would have -- which the Prosecution would have asked but we couldn't within the time limits -- we didn't think we could. But that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. But you kept on repeating certain questions, about details, especially on the armaments. So you used your time that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's right. Your Honour, because it's in the -- P174, 175, in order to make the submission at the end I have to get certain concessions from the witness and to save time, I didn't show him the documents again. So that was the point of those questions. It will become very apparent in the final trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. Ms. Registrar, could we have Exhibit P174 and 175 in front of the witness, please. Further cross-examination by Mr. Pantelic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Nikolic, would you please put one of these documents on the ELMO so that we could follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please put one of the documents, no matter which, on the ELMO. [Interpretation] It doesn't matter which.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under item 1 -- if it is easier for you to turn right and then read the document directly.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Item 1 of this document, P174, there is a word, or rather, part of the sentence, "TO company reinforced by Praga Platoon." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 2, it says, "The company again reinforced by Praga Platoon." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under 3, in the same order, it says, "TO, company reinforced by the anti-aircraft battery and armoured combat vehicle." Under 3.4 it says, "TO company Kruskovo Polje." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It means that TO units were also under your command when it came to certain combat operations.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means the following --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just say yes or no, because we have no time.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't answer it that way. This is very important. The JNA no longer exists. There is the Army of Yugoslavia as of the 27th of April. This is happening in May. So practically the TO defence is being formed and is being expanded in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, please, you've already told us that. And it's in the transcript. I'm asking you simply: In the case of combat operations for strategic or other reasons, you also had TO units and they were under your command. It's simple, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, because there are no other units. These are the only ones in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, please put the other document, P175, to the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document the second sentence under 2.1 it says, "With TO units from Plazulja and Vukovac [phoen]."

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Number 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under 2.9 it says, "Krepsic TO company will block the part of Krepsic," and so on and so forth. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the same answer applies to this document, as in the former one?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, since there is -- since the JNA is no more or its companies or its units. Then there is the TO. And that is basically my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you replied -- when you gave your answer to the Prosecutor, you several times used the words "civilian authorities" "civilian powers," so on and so forth.
