Later on you were more definite and said those were the authorities of Republika Srpska. It has to do with the police. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Because Republika Srpska had been proclaimed. It had its agencies. And I wasn't the one to say whether that was good and not right or wrong. I was only performing the military part of the job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you mentioned civilian authorities, you mean the authorities of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time you were aware that the Ministry of Police of Republika Srpska had already been set up.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that, on the basis of the -- pursuant to the decisions of the Assembly of Republika Srpska, its agencies, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as an experienced soldier and an accomplished man who has come out of the military academy, and so on and so forth, you are quite aware that the municipal assembly had absolutely no jurisdiction over the police.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, in Bosanski Samac the municipal assembly had jurisdiction of the police and they commanded the police in point of fact. As a matter of fact, I don't know. Perhaps somebody issued tasks to them, but the police could not be ranked either with the TO or the JNA, that is, the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But could it be ranked as somewhere in the hierarchy of the Ministry of Police of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since it was in this municipality, then it would be only natural for it to be in the chain of command of the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until the 19th of May, 1992, you used in some combat operation equally Lugar and Crni and Debeli, not only in this minor operation but also in some other.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used them in these two operations, clearing the roads. Except, after the crime that happened, I didn't use Lugar on the 10th in the operation conducted in the direction of Modrica. That I insisted that some men who had already appeared in bad light be excluded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As of the 17th of April, 1992 -- from the 17th of April, until the 19th of May, 1992, apart from these two operations, you also used them in other operations, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One group only participated in an operation of a breakthrough, a breakthrough the Croat -- Croatian forces between Vidovica and Kopanica, and it was all done. At that time Stevan sent that group to help out, to stop the break-through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, when was that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it before or after the massacre in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. That was long before that. That was an incident which happened before the road to Brcko and Modrica was cleared, long before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after your return to Yugoslavia, that is, Serbia, that is, after the 19th of May, 1992, did you initiate a criminal investigation against Lugar with relevant bodies?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not do it because I had no authority to do that. The TO of Republika Srpska had already been formed, and we from Yugoslavia were merely guests there. But yesterday in my statement --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll move on. All that you said, Mr. Nikolic, please rest assured is all written down. Sorry I have to interrupt you, but we are running short of time. Sorry. Can you positively say that in 1992, from April to May 1992, there was an agreement between the Republic of Serb Krajina and Republika Srpska about their mutual assistance? Have you seen this agreement? Are you aware of it, or are you just making surmises?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not get such agreements. General Sava Jankovic, my superior, told me that there was such an agreement and the rest wasn't really any of my business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Members of special units which we mentioned came from Kragujevac, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several of them. Four or five were from Kragujevac. We established that later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you come from Kragujevac too?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I come from Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you conduct combat operations at Vidovica?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is between Kopanica and Vidovica. Not I personally, the tactical group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the tactical group under your command, did it conduct operations at Kladari?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure where that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you conduct operations in Garovac?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If these are villages on the way to Modrica, then that's that. Then that is it. But otherwise, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that when Dr. Blagoje Simic attended the meeting that you described to us, that at that time he was the vice-president of the Municipality of Bosanski Samac, elected in the elections of 1990? Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how he introduced himself. Otherwise, the discussion wouldn't have made sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that Mirko Jovanovic was the president of the executive board of the Municipality of Bosanski Samac elected in the elections of 1990?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that, and he also introduced himself as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, they were their legal representatives of the Municipality of Bosanski Samac at the time.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since we yesterday discussed about the document related to the paramilitary organisation in the area of the 17th Corps and that according to that information there were no SDS formations in Samac. Today, however, you told the Prosecutor that all the three political parties were arming themselves. Are you also making conjectures about possible armaments of the SDS, or is it that you have some facts there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question was put to us by life [as interpreted]. And in the municipality we could see that all, the first, the second, the third political party were arming themselves. Whether it was not in Samac, I suppose reason for it is that they all joined the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the SDS wasn't illegally arming itself in Samac.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have that information in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were about to leave Samac to Belgrade on the 19th, to whom did you transfer the duty?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the order of the corps commander, I handed over the duty to Colonel Mico Djurdjevic, who was born in the village of Tisine Mala, I think, that is, born in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your reply to the Prosecutor you said that you knew that Blagoje and Stiv and others were members of the SDS. Now, my question to you is: Do you positively know that Stevan Todorovic was a member of the SDS? Did you ever see his admission -- his application or his membership card, or is it just a surmise?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see his application form. I didn't see anybody's application form. But this was information that was supplied to me by official agencies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then do you have any personal knowledge about who allegedly sat [Realtime transcript read in error "set"] on this -- on the Crisis Staff of the municipality? Did you see a decision or something, an order or something, or is it again a surmise on your part?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any disposition or decision, nothing like that was sent me. But from the behaviour of these people and from their statements they made, it was quite clear that they were members of Crisis Staff. Because if somebody says, "I'm a member of the Crisis Staff," then that's what it means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic. Just for the sake of clarity, could you take a look at your question, page 49, beginning line 19, because there must be something missing. You said, "Do you have any personal knowledge about who allegedly set on this?" I don't really follow what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will repeat the question. Actually, I personally cannot remember what was the exact form. I will clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the word should be "s-a-t."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question was whether you have any personal knowledge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, it's -- the interpreter was saying that the word should be "s-a-t," meaning who sat on the Crisis Staff, meaning the members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Members of the Crisis Staff, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Colonel Nikolic, at the time did you know that the Croat municipality, Omerovac [phoen] -- Samac was -- had been founded?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I said that there was hardly a place where a Crisis Staff or a municipality of sorts had not been formed, whether Serb or Croat or Muslim, it depended on the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is specific.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, I know -- specifically, I know that the Crisis Staff existed in Orasje, that a municipality of sorts was set up there, in Domaljevac, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are talking about April 1992, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, about April.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I've finished with my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, there is a matter arising out of what Mr. Pantelic asked, and I would ask leave for re-cross-examination on one point. The question was at 48/13, did you know Mirko Jovanovic was president of the executive board of the Municipality of Bosanski Samac elected in the elections of 1990? Answer: Yes, I knew that. And he also introduced himself as such. Question: In other words, they were the legal representatives of the Municipality of Bosanski Samac at the time. Answer: Yes. The witnesses -- I didn't cross-examine on this. There was no reason to. The witness's statement in paragraph 31 refers to the meeting and says that between Simic, Jovanovic, and the Bosanski Samac IO in Donji Zabar, he says, "I was told in no uncertain terms I had no jurisdiction over members of the Serbian police or members of the republic of the Serbian Krajina MUP. They were under the jurisdiction of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac. That's the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo in the process of formation and that the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo was in the process of formation had the overall responsibility for their accommodation and food and control over them. I knew I had no jurisdiction." That's something I didn't cross-examine on because I knew I had no reason to. Mr. Pantelic has raised something which is contrary to the statement and the witness has given an answer which is contrary in my submission to his statement, and I'd simply ask leave for a few moments re-cross-examination on that point, as to which is the correction version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must object. Allow me to explain. It is not in dispute in this case if we are -- if we make reference to the statute of the former Bosanski Samac municipality, where there are elections -- election results and it is not in dispute. We have -- we heard that from Mr. Izetbegovic, from Mr. Tihic, and many other witnesses who were duly elected officials among all three ethnic groups in Samac on the basis of elections in 1990, and we know that at that time Mr. Mato Nujic, a Croat, was the president, chairman of the municipal assembly, and the vice-president was Dr. Blagoje Simic, as well as the president of the executive board was Mr. Mirko Jovanovic, and the vice-president was Mr. Izet Izetbegovic. And in addition, my learned friend asked this witness in his cross-examination, who was present at that meeting, whether that was Dr. Simic, Mr. Jovanovic and Mr. Todorovic. The witness said yes, as I mentioned before. But we didn't clarify in which capacity were -- that was the basis for my questioning, although I -- as I said, this is not in dispute the official function of these people. So as a matter of principle, I object to the request of my learned friend. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will allow the Prosecution to ask the witness just one question so that he can clarify which is the right -- which is the correct version, according to the witness. Further cross-examination by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard the exchange, Mr. Nikolic. A moment ago -- I'm going to ask you a very long question. A moment ago Mr. Pantelic suggested to you that Mr. Jovanovic, Dr. Simic, and Mr. Todorovic were -- I'm sorry, that Mr. -- I'll start again. I'm sorry. He asked you, "Did you know that Mirko Jovanovic was president of the executive board of the elected Municipality of Bosanski Samac, and you said you knew that and he introduced himself to me as that. Mr. Pantelic then said --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Just for the sake of transcript and clarity. We have two elected executive board presidents, and it's the same person, Mr. Mirko Jovanovic was elected in Serbia. So in order to be precise, just make a reference that he was elected in 1990 -- on the elections 1990, because we have elections also in 1992. It's a legal question. We shall discuss that in our closing arguments. So when you make a reference of Mr. Mirko Jovanovic in capacity of president of executive board, democratically elected or whatever you want to use, just mention that it was in 1990. Otherwise, it should be a confusing area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm going to quote the exact question back to the witness. The question and answers, and I'm going to quote his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And the witness -- yes. And the witness should be allowed to say which time -- which period he's referring -- his answer refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I say, it's going to be a long question, so bear with me. If you need me to repeat anything, just stop me. Mr. Pantelic asked you, question: Do you know that when Dr. Simic attended that meeting that you described to us at the time he was the vice-president of the Municipality of Bosanski Samac elected in the elections of 1990? Were you aware of that fact. You answered: That is how he introduced himself. Otherwise, the discussion wouldn't have knead sense. Question: Did you know that Mirko Jovanovic was the president of the executive board of the Municipality of Bosanski Samac elected in the elections of 1990? Answer: Yes, I know that, and he also introduced himself as such. Question, that's Mr. Pantelic: In other words, they were their legal representatives of the Municipality of Bosanski Samac at the time? Answer: That's right. Those are the questions and answers a few moments ago. In your statement, which is in evidence here, referring to the meeting you said, in relation to the meeting at Donji Zabar, at which you gave evidence of Mr. Simic -- Dr. Simic, Mr. Jovanovic, and Mr. Todorovic attending -- or Mr. Jovanovic attending, "I was then told in no uncertain terms that I had no jurisdiction over members of the Serbian police or members of the Republic of Serbian Krajina MUP, that they were under the jurisdiction of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo in the process of formation and that the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo in the process of formation had the overall responsibility for their accommodation and food and control over them. I knew that I had no jurisdiction over them, but still I wanted to know why they had come and have some information on their objectives and tasks." That's what your statement said. That's what the questions and answers were. My question following is: How do you reconcile saying that Simic and Jovanovic were there in their capacity as elected representatives when in your statement you're implying that they are there in the capacity relating to the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac, the unelected one? How do you reconcile the two versions?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about a meeting which was held on the 12th of April, that is the time when Mr. Blagoje Simic was the vice-president of the municipality, legally elected, when Mirko Jovanovic was the president of the executive board, and there's no dispute about that. If we are talking about the jurisdiction which took place later by Mr. Todorovic, I was told actually that some preparations were going on, that some municipality -- that a Serb Municipality of Bosanski Samac was about to be put in place, and that -- and that they had the jurisdiction over these things, and that that is how it would be when the changes took effect. I cannot reproduce the whole discussion, but it is quite clear that on the 12th, at that particular moment, there were lawful representatives of the elected authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It is not recorded and translated properly what the witness said, so I just want to ask him to repeat a part when he spoke about what Todorovic said to him at that time, because this very important part is not in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I don't quite understand, Your Honours, is the statement says it was at that meeting. The witness's answer is a little bit unclear as to whether it was then or later, because the statement is fairly clear on that. And I was asking him to reconcile the capacity at which Simic, Jovanovic attended that meeting with the statement that the Serbian municipality had jurisdiction. I'm not quite sure that's the answer. There seems to be something a little bit strange --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. The witness in his answer did mention a date, so he's discussing the attendance of those people on -- he mentioned the meeting on the 12th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. The contradiction is between the statement, talking about the Serbian municipality, and the evidence that they attended in their capacity as the elected representatives. That was -- that was what my question was directed towards. And I'm not sure the answer clarifies it. But I was only allowed one question, so I don't think I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. But that is a matter for submission, isn't it, if there is a contradiction in what he has just said and what he said in his 92 bis statement. Because in his answer, he has given a date, and that is material.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked in what capacity -- it's not quite clear from the answer -- in what capacity Dr. Simic, Mr. Jovanovic, and Mr. Todorovic, who was there, attended that meeting? That's as far as I want to go, in what capacity he now says they attended the meeting. Could I ask that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, prior -- I don't have a problem with that. But please, could my learned friend can clarify that with the witness, what he said when he mentioned Todorovic in his last answer, because I said due to some problems in the interpretation we didn't -- we heard that in B/C/S language but we didn't hear that very important issue. I don't want to -- to coach the witness. That's why I'm not going over what he said. I don't know. It's very important thing. It's not in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let's do it this way: Can the witness tell the Trial Chamber or repeat his evidence as to what Mr. Todorovic told him, the point Mr. Pantelic says is not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. This is the core of the matter. This was a meeting that was held on the 12th of April. I said that after this unit landed, I invited Todorovic to this meeting and Mijak, commander of the 1st Detachment. In addition to them, Mr. Blagoje Simic came and Mr. Mirko Jovanovic came and some other people too. I said that in my statement yesterday. So that is not in dispute. I knew -- I knew -- and that is how they introduced themselves, but I also knew that, that Mr. Simic was vice-president of the municipality. I knew that Mirko Jovanovic was president of the executive board. I knew that Todorovic at that moment in the 1st Detachment carried out the duties of Assistant Commander for Security and Intelligence matters and that Mijak was carrying out the duty of commander of that detachment. There were some other persons there, too, and of course there was Mr. Radovanovic and Mr. Djordjevic, that is, Crni and Debeli. There is no denial. I asked -- I knew what their positions were, and I asked whether they came in that capacity, and they said yes. Also yesterday I said that Mr. Todorovic did most of the talking. And inter alia, he said that he was the one who invited these people, that he would be the one who would be the head of MUP, that is to say, of the future Serb Municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo in the process of formation, that they were under his jurisdiction, that he would take care of them, that he would accommodate them, that held support logistically and that I had nothing to do with that. So this shows that there was already an idea, a moment, a time when there would be a Serbian municipality created. And then, on the other hand, these are the legal representatives of the authorities, if I managed to explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. I think that has been cleared by the witness. Any re-examination, Mr. Pisarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Re-examined by Mr. Pisarevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, I'm just going to put a few questions to you. You said when you testified here that you met Mr. Zaric towards the end of October 1991. Can you tell the Trial Chamber here when your contacts with Mr. Zaric became more regular, more direct, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday in my statement I said that I met Mr. Zaric in October, that I met him on purpose with certain instructions and some information about his work and his merits and so on. These contacts were relatively few. They were intensified when the detachment was first established and when the 4th Detachment was finally established on the 5th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly? Did you say 2002 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask that Mr. Pisarevic speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, please speak close to the microphone. And also remember to pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday that on one occasion Colonel Djurdjevic was at a meeting representing the 4th Detachment. Can you remember which meeting this was and when it was held, something more specific about this meeting? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this meeting was somewhere around the end of April -- no, the end of March, the beginning of April. This was a meeting that was held, including the representatives of different political parties from several municipalities, Modrica, Gradacac, Orasje, Bosanski Samac, and so on. This meeting -- or rather, I was invited to this meeting by Mr. Blagoje Simic. I said that I thought I had no place there but that I would send a representative if that can be helpful or can make a contribution, since Mr. Mico Djurdjevic was from that area, he said, "I'd like to go to see what was going on, to familiarise myself with the situation and perhaps we can have some more serious information as to what can be expected," and that is how I sent Mr. Djurdjevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, you mentioned that you contacted Blagoje Simic. Did you also have contacts with Mr. Tihic and Mato Nujic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my testimony yesterday, I said -- perhaps I used an inappropriate expression. I do apologise to the Honourable Trial Chamber when I said that they were all chasing me like devils, that they were all saying that they wanted to talk to me about something. So I claimed that there was not a single person who wanted to talk to me and that I did not find the time within 24 hours to receive him and talk to him. I talked to Mr. Sulejman Tihic too. I remember that conversation from Obudovac, where he and Mr. Izo Izetbegovic were present. We talked, as usual, about all sorts of things, starting with politics and I don't know what all, and I said that the key thing at that moment was to find solutions that would not contribute to a deterioration of inter-ethnic relations. I was very pleased with what Mr. Tihic said. I think his reproach was very reasonable, and I expected him to act in a way which would help prevent this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go back to another question now. The following has been suggested to me, and I didn't hear you properly: On whose behalf did Mr. Djurdjevic go to this meeting, on behalf of the 17th Tactical Group or the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 17th Tactical Group, because Mr. Djurdjevic was my assistant commander for engineering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any contacts with Lugar, Crni, Debeli after you left Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, after the 19th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any contacts with them. I must say to the Honourable Trial Chamber that I should not be misunderstood. Mr. Pantelic put the question this way, that they are from Kragujevac and that I am from Kragujevac. I did not know a single one of them. I came to Kragujevac in 1998 [as interpreted]. I was posted there. I was in the guards units. And I literally spent all my time either in the field or in a state of combat readiness. I did not know a single one of these persons. I did not know what they were doing and I did not have any contacts with them after the 19th of May. I went to command the 152nd Mixed Brigade in Cuprija and that is where I did my job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I certainly would have asked you that. But now that you've answered, I just don't find this clear: Did I hear you properly? Did you come to Kragujevac in 1998 or 1988?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked here about the contacts and connections Mr. Zaric had in Belgrade. Do you know - and I think that you've already said this - that it was Jugoslav Maksimovic, a colonel there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The Prosecutor asked me who was my connection and who was Zaric's connection and I said that Colonel Jugoslav Maksimovic was his connection and my connection and he was one of the top people in the military security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Zaric went precisely to Jugoslav Maksimovic as a security officer.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Mr. Zaric went and conveyed all of this to him, Mr. Maksimovic brought the key people from the Security Administration to this meeting, including the head of the administration General Aleksandar Vasiljevic. And as concerns what happened in Crkvina, an official note was compiled at the security administration, and that is why I feel so bad when people ask me what I could have done, what more I could have done. I don't see what I could have done in addition to all of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked about illegal arming during the course of 1992. Did you take any measures in order to prevent illegal arming in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, all the organs of security and intelligence were engaged inter alia on one of the priority tasks, and that is precisely the prevention of illegal weapons and ammunitions being brought in. There was an agreement between Delimustafic, Minister of the Interior, and the head of the Security Administration, General Vasiljevic. This agreement was made to place joint checkpoints of the military police and the civilian police in order to prevent all of this. It is in this connection that I went to talk to Vinko Dragicevic who was head of MUP. We could not reach any agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If necessary I can explain what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You have already spoken about this. This is in your statement. So I just wanted to ask you: So did you place these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I placed a checkpoint at a better place, if I can put it that way, better than the place where the police of Bosanski Samac had placed its checkpoints. So I got hold of all illegal deliveries. When they understood that regardless of whatever they were doing these deliveries came into my hands, nevertheless, then they came to see me and they said, "Oh, we want our checkpoint to be there too," and I said, "There is no dispute about that --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. I didn't ask anything about checkpoints. I asked about information about illegal arming leading to the interrogation of people who were imprisoned afterwards. That was as far as I went. That was the extent of my cross-examination. It doesn't arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic, the Prosecution -- the Prosecution is right. There was no discussion on checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. It's not specifically checkpoints, but what was said was what the colonel as the commander did in order to prevent illegal arming. So the placement of checkpoints is one of the things that was done in order to stop illegal import of weapons, military weapons, into Bosnia-Herzegovina. And now I'm going to ask about the collection of information. This is going to be my last question, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Both you and Mr. Makso Simeunovic, what were you guided by when you sent Mr. Zaric, or rather, when you ordered Mr. Zaric to go to the police station and to conduct interviews with certain persons that he deemed necessary? What did you want to establish in this way?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since it had already been established that at the police station there was a certain number of detainees from conversations from Todorovic it was said to me that these were people who were involved in smuggling and other illegal activities. If that was so, then I said it would be a good thing if Zaric went. Perhaps he is going to learn something from them that we are also interested too and these are the kind of people that they have there. And we were only actually interested in knowing whether there were some people there who took part in the illegal arming and transfer of military equipment from Croatia to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was our main task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you interested in which officers of the JNA were included in that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've already said this, that on the basis of the information that we had sent and not only we, all members of the 17th Corps were engaged in this particular work, and on this basis some people were later indicted for having taken part in illegal arming. Actually, it was easy to establish this. We knew where each rifle had left. When you find this rifle elsewhere and then you see who sold this person that rifle and then the matter is resolved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nikolic, just a couple of questions. The first relates to something that you mentioned to the Prosecutor. It's page 58, lines 13 to 15, where concerning the meeting on April the 12th, 1992 you state, I quote: "So this shows that there was already an idea, a moment, a time when there would be a Serbian municipality created." And what I'm wondering is: At that time, can you recall whether based on the conversation with the persons at the meeting and based on the arrival of the two helicopters with the armed men, do you recall whether you anticipated an imminent takeover of Bosanski Samac, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have understood this question. On the basis of the behaviour and the statements and the way in which Mr. Todorovic spoke, I had in a way taken this to be a suggestion that there were some changes that were in the making and that he would be this new chief of police and that this group is his concern and that he would think about that. That is why I made the kind of statement I made a while ago, because I felt that something was in the making. I felt that something was going on. I don't know if I've been clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you. And did you -- did you report on this meeting and these thoughts that you had, that you've just mentioned, up the JNA chain of command to your -- you know, your immediate superiors?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have understood the question. Every day from Tactical Group 17 a regular combat report went, a regular operative report went, until the combat operations started. And when the combat operations started, then a regular combat report, in which I, inter alia, was supposed to mention under one particular item what I had done a particular day, who I had talked to, what I had done, and I was duty-bound to give an assessment of my own. My assessment was more or less as follows: That in the entire territory, regardless of whether it was covered by Croats, regardless of whether it was covered by Muslims or Serbs, there is a tendency - and I already said that in my previous statement - that is to say, that they were all making Crisis Staffs and they all had this tendency of making their mini municipalities, et cetera, and that is how I put it to my commander. That's what I wrote in my report to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And lastly, Mr. Nikolic: In your -- in your statement, you mention that -- in paragraph 34 that after Mr. Antic or Mr. Zaric met with you on the 17th of April, 1992, that you issued orders that the 4th Detachment wasn't to get involved in the situation in Bosanski Samac town and so on. And I would just like to have a clear picture. Why did you issue that order that they should not get involved?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have understood the question. You see, if I were to get involved in everything that was going on in ethnic communities, in existing municipalities, then the work of the 17th Operative Group would be reduced to coup d'etats, mini coups, vis-a-vis one government or another government. We were ordered to avoid this at any cost. What kind of government would be set up was not our problem, our problem was that we should do our part of the job, namely the three tasks that I refer to. If there is a conflict that, we should try to prevent it, to separate the sides, et cetera. And that is why I did not want to bring the detachment into a situation that would make them deal with internal matters of government. And since the detachment had a mixed composition, you can imagine what this would have led to. Then I would have practically been the one who had started an inter-ethnic conflict in Bosanski Samac. That is why I wanted the detachment to remain on the sidelines and to carry out only the assignments that they were supposed to carry out. After all, that is what was suggested to me by my commander. And in these many talks that we had, there was a general position that we should not interfere into what was being done by politics and that we should carry out our military tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a very short question to you,

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radovan Antic gave evidence here before this Chamber a month ago about what you told him and Mr. Zaric in the morning of the 17th of April, 1992 about a phone call you had received from Dr. Blagoje Simic in the very early morning hours of the 17th of April, 1992. Mr. Antic's statement differs, if my memory serves me well, in certain respects from what you told us yesterday. So now I'm kindly asking you: Could you be so kind, to the best of your recollection, to tell us once more what Dr. Blagoje Simic in fact told you about what had happened in Bosanski Samac in the -- during the night 16th and 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have understood. Dr. Blagoje Simic called me and said that a Crisis Staff had been established that represents the Serb Municipalities of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo in the process of formation, and that certain actions and measures were taken in order to take over authority in Bosanski Samac, and that this process was already underway and that literally it had been almost brought to an end. When Mr. Antic and Mr. Zaric came to see me, they were quite worked up. I don't know if this is the right expression. And they wanted to see what the position of the detachment was. They wanted to get involved in some way. And I said that I thought that the best solution was that we obey what the corps commander said and that we should not get involved in this, believing that there would probably be other places too where somebody would take over in one way or the other, and then this would involve the military in government affairs. And I literally insisted on fleeing from any kind of meddling in government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have a question, Your Honour, on the basis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. You had the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I have, according to the rules, Your Honour. May I respectfully remind you that after the questions of the Bench --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. But what has been raised which hasn't been raised before. In connection with what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just one question, with regard to my client, Your Honour, on the basis of discrepancies -- alleged discrepancies between the statement of Mr. Antic that His Honour Judge Lindholm just mentioned and this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Perhaps I can clarify -- this matter in a very short manner. If I -- my memory serves me well, Mr. Radovan Antic said here in this room nothing else about what Mr. Blagoje Simic had said to Mr. Nikolic than Mr. Blagoje Simic told him over the phone that the Crisis Staff had decided to take over authority in Bosanski Samac. That's the difference. It's -- now when I heard it again from Mr. Nikolic, I think there is no real discrepancy. It was just two different ways of telling about the same thing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour, very shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Further cross-examination by Mr. Pantelic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Nikolic, my client, Dr. Blagoje Simic, claims that on that morning at 3.00 a.m. he did not call you at your headquarters and also that telephones in Samac were not operating. Do you agree with that position; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with the questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. I think we are now finished with your evidence. You may leave the courtroom. Yes. We shall now take our break. And I notice that we've gone over, so we shall resume at 12.55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, I would like to ask the usher to distribute these redacted versions of the statement of Mr. Antic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Examined by Mr. Pisarevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Antic, during the proofing for your testimony today, we have already spoken about this technical part of your testimony. I would like to ask you, therefore, to remember what we said so that your testimony can be taken down as best possible. You know very well that you gave a statement. Your statement is certified. It is in the hands of the Trial Chamber and other participants in the case. And it was decided that you will testify here under items 15, 19, 24, and 25. For the record, kindly state your full name.

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: My name is Vaso Antic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, you've described the events of the 17th of April, 1992. You've also talked about the events that took place on the 11th of April, 1992. I would like to ask you a question regarding a phone call. Did anybody call you on the telephone on the 18th of April, 1992 early in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you like me to stand up?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. You can remain seated.

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 18th of July [as interpreted], I got a phone call around 12.00, between 1200 hours and 1300 hours. I heard the voice tell me, "This is the Crisis Staff. You have a mission and you must carry out an order of the Crisis Staff. You have to make sure that the Radio Bosanski Samac becomes operational." I then proceeded to ask a few questions, but I was not given the permission to ask these questions. They told me that I must carry out my task, I should not ask any questions, but I nevertheless wanted to know who was on the other side of the line and who had ordered that, who is the representative of the Crisis Staff on the telephone. And I was told, "You know who is the president of the Crisis Staff, and the Crisis Staff ordered the following," and it was the president of the Crisis Staff, Mr. Blagoje Simic. That very moment I decided to go to the radio station. The radio station was approximately from 300 to 400 metres from my apartment. There were shots that could be heard in the city. But I decided to walk to the radio station. I did not have my car with me. My wife took the car. She brought the children to Gajovi was the village where I was born and this is where I had my house and this is where my wife went with my children and that's why she took the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please -- if Your Honours please, in the English transcript, line 6, this is supposed to have happened on the 18th of July, according to this witness. I wonder if that's a mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to thank my learned colleague. This is why I stopped the witness because I was just about to ask him that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm terribly sorry. It is true. It was the month of April. Yes, it was the 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the event you described to us a few moments ago took place in April, it was the 18th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you proceeded to go to Radio Samac. Where were they? Where was Radio Samac, in what building?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: The office of Radio Samac was in the memorial centre called Trifunovic Uco. I got to the radio station and I saw that everything had been overturned in the radio station, going from the archives, the records that were in a certain area, all the drawers were full of archive material and everything was overturned. Nobody explained to me why this material was overturned, but through my experience I knew how to turn on the radio. I knew how to do it. I wanted to know if the transmitter was operational. And when I turned on the radio, I found out that the ultra short waves were operational and that it can cover only a very small area of the city, whereas the transmitter that was on a elementary school had been burnt down and that's why it was no longer operational.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you indeed turn on Radio Samac and were you able to broadcast programmes?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: I was the only one at Radio Samac, the only person working, the only staff member. And in fact, at the memorial centre I found about 15 soldiers in uniform, and I asked them, "Why is the situation such as it is?" I told them that I had turned on the radio station and then I broadcasted some music. Sometime later on --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just slow down, please. Right. So then you turned on the radio and you were able to play some music? Up until the moment you arrived there, was Radio Samac operational and was it operational on the 17th and on the 18th of April, the day when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: I was the director and I was the responsible editor of the radio station. The last broadcast of a programme took place on the 16th of April. And because of the situation in the city, nobody came to work. That's why the radio was not at all working up until the 18th, up until the moment when I got there in the early hours of the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that 18th -- after the 18th, rather, did you continue going to work at Radio Samac?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the 18th, when the programme became operational, when I was able to start it, it was actually a temporary programme. I didn't have the necessary staff. I could not broadcast the normal programme, and this is why it was sort of a temporary solution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you call people who had been working prior to that date at the radio station? Did you call some journalists? Did you call some people?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: That very moment I called the Crisis Staff and I wanted to know if these people were who supposed to work with me could come back to the radio station, because I said I could not work alone. They told me, "Yes, that is possible." And that very moment I was told to get in touch with Stevan Todorovic and Mr. Simeunovic, if I recall correctly, and this is how I got in touch with them. I was told that I can call the people for whom I think they can help with regards to the editing of a regular broadcasting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you call?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: I called Ljubomir Cordasevic. He was a journalist. He had worked previously as a foreign correspondent with the radio station. Then I called Miroslav Vujic [phoen] and then Angelina Vasovic and Stojan Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any technicians at the radio station at the time?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: I immediately called the people -- I told you that I had had a technician earlier -- I had a technician who was Croatian from Prud and he was not able to come, and then I remembered that he had worked -- that somebody else had worked earlier at the radio station, Pasaga Tihic. He was a good technician. I had asked him can I hire him, would he come and work as a technician. And Stevan Todorovic said to me that "You can hire that man," but he said, "You are responsible for him." I then said, "I cannot be responsible for anybody." And then he told me, "Well, you can drive him every morning to the SUP or the MUP and in the evening you have to bring him in so he can report to the MUP," and I agreed to it, that I would bring him twice a day and that I would bring him to the MUP but that -- and this is the only way he could come and work as a technician at the radio station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, did Pasaga Tihic come to Radio Samac?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Pasaga Tihic came immediately to the radio station. I remember I called him at home and they told me that Pasaga is not at home, that he was actually in prison. Pasaga came to work. I didn't go and get him, but he came personally, and I told him exactly what the situation was at the radio. I told him that the middle range -- the middle waves were not working but that the short waves were working for that area. And I asked him if he was able to do something so that the middle range waves or transmitter becomes operational. He said yes. He went to fix it. He stayed there for about half a day, and he fixed the transmitter and it was able to work again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Antic. That's all we want to know with regards to the arrival of Mr. Tihic at the radio station. And you covered that actually extensively in your statement. Tell us, do you remember if when we talk about Radio Samac at the beginning of May, did you get some video cassettes?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. And I remember this. I was on the field when I arrived, and when I arrived, the news reader gave me a video cassette and she told me that two police officers had brought this video cassette. Right away I called the police chief, Stevan Todorovic, and I wanted to know what this cassette was all about. He told me that it had to -- that I had to broadcast those -- actually, I should transfer these cassettes, this video cassettes, onto a regular TV, a regular tape, rather, so I asked my technician if it was possible just to transfer the portion, the speaking portion, when we hear the voice on that video cassette, if we can transfer that onto a regular cassette. Pasaga told me that yes, it was possible. He did it immediately, and he did broadcast the contents of this video or TV cassette.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what this cassette contained?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to remember the exact content. I remember the names and the people who spoke on that cassette, and I also remembered that it was a programme from Novi -- Radio or TV, rather, Novi Sad and it was broadcast earlier on TV Novi Sad. I also remember that Safet Hadzialijagic, Coner, Izet Izetbegovic also spoke on that cassette, as well as Simo Zaric, officer of the army Stevan Nikolic. And I also -- and also some other people, I don't remember their names. But I know and I can remember some details. I don't really remember all the details, but I can tell you the following: I remember that there was a speech made by Stevan Nikolic and he was calling soldiers to answer the call-up, and I remember that Simo Zaric said that they were able to find the trace of the arming of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Do you remember if on that cassette there was an interview between Mr. Tihic and Mr. Alijagic?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Omer Nalic. Rather, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Omer Nalic also gave a speech there, but I don't remember the exact content of the speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pasaga Tihic, therefore, transferred that onto a regular cassette, audio cassette, from a video cassette. Did you broadcast that programme?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. We broadcasted that programme five to six times, not on the same day but at various moments and on different days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those people were not present at the time when you were broadcasting this cassette.

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: No, they were not present, meaning that we did broadcast this programme without their presence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Antic. Tell us, please, did you go to work every day?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without you and without your permission, it was impossible to broadcast any programme; right?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: May I please clarify?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: I was still the director of the radio station, the main editor, but I must say the following - and this is important - I was, therefore, the editor-in-chief, and Stevan Todorovic was the president of the executive committee of the radio, and Simeon Simic and both of them told me that I cannot broadcast absolutely anything without their approval, especially not if there was an important interview. Then they told me -- they gave me some names and they said that those names should not have access to the radio station. I remember Zarko Krstanovic, that was one of the names, Pero Vasiljevic, Simo Zaric, said that these people should not come to the radio station. And I really had to carry out that order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me if, as of the 16th of April, 1992 and up until all that period during which you were the editor-in-chief, did Simo Zaric participate personally in any programme broadcasted by Radio Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: It is my duty to remember, and I do, of course. During that period, during those six months when I was the editor-in-chief, because I was dismissed afterwards, Simo Zaric never -- was never present at the radio station. If you will allow me, I would just like to add one more sentence: During my work, during those six months, I really tried hard to tell the truth to this unfortunate people, but I had horrendous problems because of it and this is one of the reasons why I could not decide to do anything that was not allowed for me to do during that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Please tell us, how did you -- how did they explain to you the fact that they had forbid Mr. -- these people to -- how did they explain why was Mr. Zaric prohibited from appearing on the radio station?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew rather well Stevan Todorovic and Simeon Simic, so I did ask them why are you not allowing some people to speak on the radio, not because of them but because I wanted to know that. And I was told, "No, we shall not admit any Commies or balija relatives, those related to balijas, to speak on the radio."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that word "Commies," was that the term used for people who were communists or what?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a pejorative term which is used to this day. This was a pejorative term for people who were prominent members of the League of Communists and who held certain offices before the war, and it was even said, "Well, we've had enough of Zarics, so let us take rest."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does it mean "balija relatives"? What is that supposed to mean?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose because Simo Zaric's wife is of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. If you could take a look at page 79, line 4. I don't quite understand the quotation, "Well, we've had enough of Zarics, so let us take rest." It must be a translation problem, I think. Could you clarify what it means or what it's supposed to mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, you've heard the question of Her Honour Judge Williams. Was it said Zarics -- "we've had enough of Zarics. Let them have a rest" or "let him have a rest"? Was it singular or plural?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: No, I think we've had enough of them so let them have a rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the Zarics take a breath?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Zarics take a breath.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Simo Zaric ever read out names of people who should be arrested?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Well, how could he do that if he had no access?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that Simo Zaric could not read anything on air, that he could not threaten any Muslims or Croats in Samac with arrests or anything?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: No. While I was editor-in-chief, during those five or six months while I was there, no, he never once did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a programme devoted to Serbs arrested -- captured in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: During that time - and I must again refer to the period when I was there - I do not recall any such programme, and I would remember it had there been any special programme devoted to that on Radio Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any news programmes?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps there could have been something on the news about it, but there were no special programmes about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Antic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Pantelic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Antic. I am lawyer Pantelic and I am counsel for Dr. Blagoje Simic. Mr. Antic, as a journalist of long-standing and as the editor of Radio Samac and a man who is well abreast of things that go on, will you tell us, please, tell us if Radovan Karadzic came to Samac in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: I was there all the time, that is the town where I was born. I was there throughout. And I'll tell you something about it later. But I affirm positively that at that time Radovan Karadzic did not come. I remember, however, and I wanted to attend a meeting where Mr. Alija Izetbegovic came to a meeting, the meeting that I wanted to attend. But at that time it wasn't public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I getting your meeting right? Does this mean that from October 1991 to April 1992 Radovan Karadzic did not visit Samac?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: He didn't, except without my knowledge. But I affirm only what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will agree with me that a visit by one of the leaders in Bosnia-Herzegovina would not -- could not have passed unnoticed in such a small town; wouldn't you say so?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Well, I would have surely. I did my best to keep abreast of all the meetings, desirous of informing the public objectively, because I was writing for an independent newspaper who were willing to publish my articles, and I'm quite sure that I would have covered that event had I known about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the staff council having its seat in the heating plant?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. The Crisis Staff had its seat in the heating plant. But I wouldn't know at what time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Because we are pressed for time, will you please try to answer yes or no, and if we need any more detailed answer, then I'll tell you so.

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the seat of the executive board of the Municipality of Samac was?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: In the municipal -- in the building of the municipal hall of the present municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you visit the executive council within the framework of your job?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because we had to apply for all the resources that we needed from the president of the executive board, Mr. Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you communicate with Dr. Blagoje Simic personally in whatever regard, concerning your work, of course?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the early days. But when we were told that everything that had to do with the radio, that we had to address it with Stevan Todorovic, then I did it with them and then I did it through them except when I wanted to make an interview with Dr. Blagoje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Dr. Blagoje Simic use the waves, Radio Samac, to address some discriminatory messages against the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: No, and I claim this with responsibility, and I can say that because I was really endeavouring to inform the public objectively. I need to add two or three sentences about a programme that I had introduced without anyone's knowledge. It was called "Missing and lost," and I never received any comments, any negative comments about that, because I was trying to bring together families which had been separated for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you use the waves, Radio Samac, to broadcast orders about the compulsory white ribbons that the non-Serb population of Samac was to wear?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: No. Radio Samac never aired such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you broadcast on Radio Samac any proclamation about the prohibition of the assembly of more than two or three Croats or Muslims in Samac?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: No. But I did read something about that on chestnut trees. On the trunks there would be such prohibitions, prohibiting the assembly of larger groups. But radio never aired such prohibition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, I presume you are aware that Simo Zaric wrote a book on The Hague crucifix, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will read out to you a part of it which deals with Day D, as he called it, the 17th of April, 1992. So will you please now tell me what you think about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, many things are being taken out of the context. Can this fragment be put before the witness and have the witness read it and then if somebody wants to ask questions, then let him only then ask the questions about what the book says.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are also asking that the relevant passage be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in order to speed up proceedings, I will simply read the passage and then the witness can say whether he's agreed or not. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can read it -- read it slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Simo Zaric says that he had written -- that he wrote the proclamation of the 4th Detachment on the 17th of April. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Proclamation to the citizenry --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... 220 of his book, B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Proclamation to the citizenry, which I wrote that morning, pursuant to the order of our command on the assessment of the new authorities was a complete failure, even worse than that. It was read on the radio only once and prohibited immediately. "Briefly pointing out at the duty of the citizens to hand over the weapons and to know what had happened overnight, how, and `what the actual situation had set in' that the Serb power had been introduced in Samac. I went `too far,' anticipating an impossible further evolution of inter-ethnic relations." That is an accurate assessment of the events, that which Zaric says. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the 17th of April, the proclamation of the 4th Detachment was read out in Samac, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit D28/4, please. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, for that last passage of evidence to make sense to you, the -- Mr. Pantelic should have specified - and I think he was trying to specify this - that the proclamation was read out in Samac by Mr. Zaric. That's what I understood his question to be. And with respect, he hasn't got an answer to his question. The witness says he doesn't remember the date. But if I'm correct in what the question was intended to be, he hasn't got an answer to the question either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, tell us, was this proclamation that was read out by Mr. Simo Zaric? You do not remember that, or was it the 4th Detachment proclamation? Tell us what you remember. You have the proclamation in front of you. So that could jog your memory, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we have this document on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The proclamation was read out by the announcer, but I really do not remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you have no reasons to doubt what Mr. Simo Zaric says in his book, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, in your statement, 92 bis in paragraph 4 you say that until 1995 you worked as a journalist and that then, that is, in 1995, Stevan Todorovic, the president of the administrative board notified you that you were no longer working there. Isn't that so? Or you can look at your statement.

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: No, there's no need for that. I know it by heart, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the end of the war, when the Dayton Accords were signed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us cut it shorter.

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Please, I didn't finish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A very simple matter. In 1995, as a journalist you were told that you no longer worked in Samac; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... a part of paragraph 4 is beyond the indictment. There is not any relevance to these proceedings. I respectfully move this Trial Chamber to strike out this part, which is the end --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is paragraph 4 of the statement of this witness. And last three sentences should be struck out, beginning with the words, "That day Stevan Todorovic called me," et cetera, et cetera, because there is not any relevance to the proceedings. It's beyond the time frame of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That will be taken care of when assessing the evidence. We don't need to strike out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's just for the record. Thank you very much. Can I -- just to have a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, thank you. I've finished with this do you mean. Thank you very much. My learned friend just -- he was kind to inform me. Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My client, Dr. Blagoje Simic, sent me the following instruction: He says that the Crisis Staff did not order to activate the radio and to read proclamations but that it was done by Simo Zaric and the 4th Detachment. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: No. Most emphatically, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next position of my client is that Simo Zaric in 1992, especially in those early months, was very much present at Radio Samac, always commenting on things. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I've finished with the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution, any cross-examination? MR. DI FAZIO: I certainly do have some, if Your Honours please. Might I just enquire as to what you see happening with respect to our schedule and timetable over the next few days, and in particular today and tomorrow. The only reason I ask is this: I'm given to understand that there are no further witnesses beyond this particular witness. If we've got time to finish this witness this afternoon, certainly I'd be happy and willing to embark on my cross-examination now. However, if there is a -- the prospect of resuming this after the long break, then in my submission no useful purpose could be served by my launching five minutes into my cross-examination, and I'd like to do that after the long break. So I'm in Your Honours' hands. I'm comply with whatever you want. But I respectfully suggest that if there's going to be a long break, let me start after the long break. We're only going to lose five -- five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I just suggest something in relation to what the Prosecution just said? It is also in the interest of our clients who find this most difficult to wait for more than an hour and a half. Since the Trial Chamber ruled that the cross-examination could go on for an hour and a half, it would be useful if the Prosecutor would tell us whether that would be the time limit. I think that all the participants would agree if just a short break would be made or if we would just continue, because that is what they find the most difficult at all. Perhaps the Prosecutor could tell us whether he would stick to this time frame allotted to him by the Trial Chamber so the Trial Chamber could rule and this would not be to the detriment of our clients' health. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll be sticking to whatever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought according to the ruling the Prosecutor had one hour. MR. DI FAZIO: That's what I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let me find out from the registry assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll continue in the afternoon, hopefully at 14.15. MR. DI FAZIO: Fine. Thank you, Your Honours. I'm happy with that. Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, you were a member of the 4th Detachment, you were a private in the 4th Detachment, and you joined the 4th Detachment in early 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You joined the 4th Detachment following orders to mobilise and -- not mobilise, to report for duty.

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 18th of April, 1992 you received instructions to go to the radio station and start getting it into working order.

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know, don't you, that the 4th Detachment was mobilised on the 17th of April and that it received orders to take up positions on the Bosna and the Sava River and also to start the collection of weaponry held by citizens?

utterances.speaker: VASO ANTIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that, because I never specifically determined my duties in the 4th Detachment because I was involved in my work as a journalist. But I was a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you were a member of the 4th Detachment. You were duty-bound to follow the orders of your commander, and you weren't a member of the 4th Detachment just for fun, were you?
